In April Mrs. Okafor caught her toe on a raised edge, went down on one knee, and broke a jar of honey across three bricks. The city put the walk on its list of repairs. By June the list had not moved, and Mr. Fenn, who lived at number 11 and taught shop at the high school, announced that the street would fix the walk itself on the last Saturday of the month.

He arrived that morning with a wheelbarrow of sand, two rented tampers, a long level, and a plan drawn on graph paper. The roots would be trimmed where they could be, the old bricks lifted and stacked, a fresh bed of sand laid and pounded hard, and the bricks set back in their old pattern. "Flat and tight," he said, tapping the paper. "That's all a walk has to be."

Ana was twelve, and her job was stacking. She pried each brick loose with a flat bar, knocked the old sand off it, and carried the bricks four at a time to the piles on the grass. Her grandmother had come over from number 7 with a folding chair and a thermos of tea, and she lifted nothing. She watched the bricks come up, one row after another, and she watched the dark streaks in the damp sand beneath them, which all ran the same way, toward the street.

Late in the morning she borrowed a ball of string from Mr. Fenn's toolbox. She had Ana hold one end against the bottom step of number 7, walked the other end out to the curb, and pulled it tight, crouching beside it and squinting along its length for a long time. Then she had Ana drive two stakes to hold it and went back to her chair.

Mr. Fenn found the string when he reached number 7 with his wheelbarrow. "What's this for?" he asked. Ana's grandmother said only that the old walk had always leaned a little toward the street, and she asked whether Ana might lay the sand and bricks in front of number 7 along the string. Mr. Fenn said the lean was the roots' doing. Then he laughed and waved a hand. "It's your front," he said. "Lay it however you like." He wheeled his sand on to number 9, where he raked it out and laid his level across it again and again until the bubble sat dead center.

Ana did as her grandmother said, packing the sand higher by the step and lower by the curb, and by dark the last brick on the street was in. That night it rained. In the morning a puddle the size of a doormat stood on the new bricks in front of numbers 9 and 11, while the walk in front of number 7 was already drying. Mr. Fenn stood at the edge of the puddle with his coffee for a while. Then he came up the steps of number 7 with his graph paper and a pencil and asked Ana's grandmother how much a walk ought to lean.

In the last week of October my father
goes down to the cellar for the other windows,
the ones that spend the summer stacked on edge
behind the furnace, numbered on their frames
in pencil gone silver with handling,
one through fourteen, one for every window in the house.

I carry the small ones. He carries the tall ones
flat against his chest, like a man holding a door
that has come off in a wind. We lean them
along the porch rail in order, and I wash them
with newspaper and a bucket of warm water
until the glass squeaks and the yard comes back.

Every year there is a wasp or two
asleep in a corner of a frame, dry as a leaf.
Every year my father lifts it out with a fingernail,
sets it on the rail, and says, Go on,
as if it had somewhere it was expected.

Then the ladder. He climbs, and I hand up
the window whose number matches the one
penciled on the sill, because nothing else will fit.
The house has settled, he says, a little crooked
in its own way at every opening,
and each pane was cut to one crooked place
and remembers it, the way a shoe remembers a foot.

By dark the house is wearing its second skin.
The street goes quiet the way a room goes quiet
when someone shuts the door on a party.
The furnace starts. We sit in the kitchen and listen
to the wind try every window and find each one
already answered, twice.

The fall I was in seventh grade, my mother came to her first parent-teacher conference at Hillcrest Middle School, and I came with her to translate. She had arrived from Belo Horizonte two years before, and her English was the English of the bakery where she worked the morning shift: prices, the names of breads, good morning, have a nice day. For anything longer, she had me.

I had translated for her before, at the pharmacy and once at the bank, and I was good at it. I liked the moment when an adult turned from my mother to me and began talking to me as if I were the grown-up in the room. I had learned to keep my face still while I did it, and to say everything in the same even voice, the way the interpreters did on the news.

Mr. Dawes, my math teacher, had my grades open on a laptop when we sat down. He was kind and tired and spoke slowly for my mother's sake, which meant that every word landed. Lucas is clearly capable, he said. But he has missed five homework assignments since September, and he did not turn in the project on fractions.

In Portuguese, I told my mother that Mr. Dawes said I was very capable and sometimes forgot my homework.

My mother nodded. She asked me to ask him whether I talked too much in class, which was what my teachers in Brazil had always said, and I asked, and Mr. Dawes laughed and said the opposite, that I hardly spoke at all. That one I translated exactly. Then he turned the laptop toward us so we could see the column of grades, and he thanked us for coming.

We walked to the bus stop without talking. On the bus, my mother took a pen from her bag and wrote a row of numbers on the back of her hand: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0. Then she held the hand out to me, palm down, and said in Portuguese that a zero looks the same in every language.

I did the five assignments that week, and the fractions project the week after. My mother never mentioned the conference again. item.passage:
Nearly every kitchen I have known has one: a drawer, usually beside the stove or under the spot where a telephone used to hang, that holds what the rest of the house refuses. Open it and you will find rubber bands gone stiff, a birthday candle, two keys to unknown locks, a takeout menu from a restaurant that closed, a screw, a tape measure that retracts only halfway, and a single battery whose charge is a matter of faith.

The professional organizers who write books about tidiness have a firm rule for this drawer. Empty it onto the counter, they say, and keep only what you have used in the past year. Everything else goes in the trash. Some of them go further and say the drawer should not exist at all, since a thing without a proper place is a decision you have failed to make.

I have read that rule perhaps forty times in perhaps forty books, and every time it makes me want to throw the book in the drawer. The rule measures a thing by how often it is used, and that is exactly the wrong measure for most of what the drawer holds. A spare key is worth keeping precisely because it sits unused. The screw is waiting for the day the bookshelf wobbles. The candle is for a cake that has not been baked yet. Judged by the calendar, they are clutter; judged by what they are for, they are insurance.

The organizers are right about one thing. The drawer is a place for decisions that have been put off. But putting a decision off is often the wisest thing to do with it. When I find an unfamiliar key on the floor, I cannot know today whether it opens the shed, the bike lock or some door I have forgotten. The drawer lets me keep the question open without keeping it in my hand.

There is a cost, of course. Sooner or later the drawer jams on a spatula, and I have to dig through it to find the scissors. Once or twice a year I do sort it, and I throw away what has clearly lost its chance: the dead batteries, the menus from restaurants long gone. The keys stay. One of them had been rattling in there for at least ten years when it turned out to open my grandfather's tool chest, which had been locked since before I was born, and I have not been able to read the organizers' rule the same way since.

On the afternoon of July 9, 1893, a hailstorm crossed Varnby Township from west to east in about twenty minutes. It left a path roughly two miles wide in which the wheat, a week from harvest, lay flat and broken. Forty-one farms lost most of a year's crop. Farms a mile to the north lost almost nothing.

Insurance against hail could be bought in 1893, but only from companies in distant cities, and few farmers in Varnby carried it. The premiums were high, and the stories about those companies were worse: agents who sold policies in the spring and could not be found in August, claims that took a year to settle and were paid at a third of their value.

That winter a wheat farmer named Elias Brandt proposed that the township insure itself. Every member would pay into a common fund at the same rate, eight cents for each acre of grain he planted. When hail struck, a committee of three members, chosen by lot each spring, would walk the damaged fields, estimate the losses, and pay them from the fund. If the fund ran short in a bad year, every claim would be cut by the same fraction. Sixty-three farmers signed the first spring.

The summer of 1894 brought rain at the right times and clear skies at harvest. In the autumn several members asked for their money back, and when Brandt explained that the fund was meant to be kept for the next storm, eleven of them quit. Among those who stayed, the common joke was that the township had built a very handsome savings bank that paid no interest.

In June of 1895 hail came again, narrower than before but harder, and it struck nineteen member farms. The committee that year included a man named Otto Lindqvist whose own field lay in the path. He walked the other eighteen farms with his two colleagues and then asked that his own be judged by two members from the north end of the township, men who had suffered no damage. The claims came to more than the fund held, and each was paid at seventy cents on the dollar.

Seventy cents was less than the farmers had lost. It was also paid within a month, in cash, at a table in the back of Halvorsen's store, by neighbors who had walked the fields themselves. The next spring the association signed one hundred and four members, among them nine of the eleven who had quit.

Archivists who work with old motion-picture film learn to trust their noses. A can that releases a sharp whiff of vinegar when it is opened holds a reel that is coming apart. The film is almost always cellulose acetate, the plastic that, by about the middle of the twentieth century, had replaced cellulose nitrate as the base of most film. Nitrate film could catch fire easily and burn fiercely, and acetate, which burns far less readily, was sold as "safety film."

Acetate turned out to have a slow problem of its own. The plastic is cellulose, the same material as cotton fiber, with small chemical groups called acetyl groups attached along its chains. Over time, moisture in the air breaks these groups off, and each one that breaks away becomes a molecule of acetic acid, the acid that gives vinegar its smell and taste. As the groups go, the film shrinks, curls and turns brittle, and the layer that holds the picture can begin to separate from its base.

Beginning in the late 1980s, researchers at the Image Permanence Institute in Rochester, New York, set out to learn how fast this happens. Watching film decay at room temperature would have taken decades, so they sped the process up. They kept small samples of film at several high temperatures and humidities, measured how much acid built up in each over weeks and months, and then used the pattern across those conditions to estimate how the same film would behave on an ordinary shelf.

The results explained why the archivists' noses so often came too late. The reaction starts slowly, but the acid it releases speeds the reaction itself, so a film that has begun to break down produces acid faster and faster. Past a certain point the decline is steep, and the institute's estimates suggested that a film kept at ordinary room temperature and humidity could reach that point within a few decades. Kept cold and dry, the same film might last many times as long. Archivists have also found that acid vapor from one decaying reel can hasten the decay of reels stored beside it, and that a tightly sealed can, which holds the vapor in, can make matters worse.

To catch the change before anyone could smell it, the institute developed a simple test: strips of paper coated with a dye that changes color as acid accumulates. Left in a closed can for a day or more, a strip stays blue if the film is sound and shifts toward green and then yellow as the acid level rises. An archive can test thousands of reels this way and copy the yellow ones first.

Nothing yet known can turn a vinegar reel back into a sound one; cold storage only slows the clock. That is why the institute's results deserve a wider audience than archivists. In a great many basements and closets, home movies sit in tightly sealed tins at room temperature, close to the worst arrangement the tests describe, and by the time anyone notices the smell, a reel may already be past saving, with its neighbors next in line.
